Almost. There's no way to know if a measurement has occurred. Basically, quantum teleportation is a way to transmit a quantum state or qubit, superposition intact and all. It works like this:

  1. You create an entangled photon pair and send one half of the pair to your recipient. This means that any quantum state you imprint on photon A is also imprinted on photon B.
  2. You have a qubit in a specific superposition state. Measuring it will destroy the information. You entangle it with A so you imprint it upon the photon pair. This has several important consequences.
  3. The entanglement between A and B is now broken. The original qubit at the end of A is destroyed. B is imprinted with a state from which the original can easily be regained, but the recipient has no clue this has happened, or how to recover it.
  4. The sender knows from the imprint how the receiver can recover the qubit, and sends a classical message (two bits) to the receiver to inform him that his qubit has arrived and how to recover it. This crucial step is limited by the speed of light.
  5. The qubit is recovered. Photon B now holds the exact quantum information that was to be transmitted.

And I believe that there's some way to know whether it's been examined already, so they can be used for secure communication (effectively they send a one-time pad securely to both ends).

There's no way to know if a measurement has occurred.

Here's what I was thinking of when I wrote that, quantum key distribution:

An important and unique property of quantum key distribution is the ability of the two communicating users to detect the presence of any third party trying to gain knowledge of the key. This results from a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics: the process of measuring a quantum system in general disturbs the system. A third party trying to eavesdrop on the key must in some way measure it, thus introducing detectable anomalies.

Well, you're right. What I meant was that there's no way to know if a measurement has occurred from one side only. When sending communication back and forth and (classically) comparing results, it is indeed possible to detect tampering by doing a Bell inequality test.
